what_this_is: The design for Friday's Substack exhibits (mind.the.gap, piece 904658db-4df2-4537-a0ed-ebe93e081db7): five figures, in the story's order, each answering one question a business leader would ask. A spec to draw from, not a render. Built by .cache/visual-intel/scripts/exhibits_build.py from data-final.json and derived.json; nothing published, sent or committed.

krish_asked.words: I expect some pretty heavyweight beautiful stunning visual intel as to what difference models versus thinking levels make to intelligence and how that correlates to the cost of it. I don't want you to change the article clips but I just want to make sure that those insights are enterprise-grade and available inside the substack.

story: Krish, 2026-10-17: "The story is about there being so many recent AI model releases and figuring out if that's actually important, why it's speeding up, and what choices a user is going to have to make (or what gears are going to be hidden from them in the future). It's a "mind the gap" piece remember."
article: docs/plans/2026-10-09-draft-body-v5.md (not changed; every "after" is copied from it and found exactly once)
headline: Why Claude and ChatGPT launches keep speeding up, and who will decide how hard your AI thinks

design_contract.state_of_use: A business reader on Substack, mostly on a phone (358 px column), reading the piece through; often a figure is screenshotted and shared alone.
design_contract.user_and_action: Understand, in one look per figure, whether a new model or the thinking level matters more, what each costs, and what to buy.
design_contract.governing_rule: Real Artificial Analysis rows only, by slug; every derived number has its formula; a score always with its scale; costs say what they are.
design_contract.data_truth: Sparse where Artificial Analysis is: Google has one ranged model and its Low has no cost; ChatGPT's app settings are not mapped; Haiku costs understated.
design_contract.materiality: Material: new figures for a piece Krish has signed off. He sees the rendered set before it goes into the page.
design_contract.brand_and_voice: makeyourmindup house style from config/studio.json via scripts/pages/brand.py; mind.the.gap accent; krish-voice rules for every word.
design_contract.authority: Design spec only. Rendering, the pack and posting are later steps; posting is his.
design_contract.proof: Each render passes scripts/pages/card.py at 1360 wide (phone floor), is looked at at full size and at 358 px, and is checked against this file.

canvas.height: per exhibit, set by its content (see each size); nothing clipped, no inner scroll

design_system.device: One device for all five, in the channel style (CHANNEL_HEADINGS): a numbered kicker "EXHIBIT N · SOURCE · DATE", then one heading of one shape, a short claim (or, for the last, a promise) naming the real products, then a one-line standfirst saying what is measured. Every chart labels its marks directly; no separate legend box.
words: Thinking level is the term on every exhibit. Exhibit 2, the first data exhibit, defines it as what Anthropic calls effort and OpenAI calls reasoning.
Settings are printed with Artificial Analysis's names: Non-reasoning (thinking off), Low, Medium, High, Xhigh (extra high, glossed once per exhibit), Max.
No car, gear or badge words on any exhibit: the article carries the car; the charts carry the real setting names (ANALOGY_IN_SCRIPTS_ONLY).
No em dashes or en dashes; British spelling; "times" in words, not a multiplication sign; a score always with its scale (PLAIN_SCORES).

cost_measure.printed_as: cost per task: Artificial Analysis's average cost to run one of its test tasks, in US dollars, at list prices
cost_measure.why: Every Artificial Analysis dollar figure and multiple in the article is cost per task ($5.98 v $0.55; "about two and a half times as much per task"; "another four and a half times"; "about 11 times"; "28% more"; "less than half the cost per task"), and Friday's video cards use cost per task too. An exhibit printed beside those sentences on the full-test-set cost would show 1.89, 5.35, 10.12, 1.45 and 0.38 times instead, so the reader would see two sets of numbers for one claim. data-final.json allows either, if the exhibit says which.
cost_measure.alternative: cost_usd (what it cost Artificial Analysis to run its full test set once, US dollars, at list prices) is kept beside every plotted row as cost_usd_full_test_set, so any exhibit can be redrawn on it. Every pattern claimed below holds on both measures (checked: see checks).

score_basis: The API's one-decimal score (data-final.json score; derived.json points_gained) throughout. Artificial Analysis's pages print whole numbers; never round a one-decimal figure again (29.5, 34.5 and 33.5 are rounding traps).

exhibits.after: Start with why your eyes are on the name at all, because while we watch the names, the setting that decides your answer gets chosen out of sight. Look at how often the names change. Anthropic, which makes Claude, launched Claude Opus 4.8 in May, Claude Opus 5 in July and Claude Opus 5.5 in September, with Sonnet, Fable and Haiku versions alongside. OpenAI's release notes climb from GPT-5.1 last November to GPT-6.1 Sol at the end of September. OpenAI even says a model will "generally remain available in ChatGPT for 90 days after a successor is released." Ninety days, and then the next name takes over.

exhibits.source_line: Source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, read 17 Oct 2026. Cost per task: its average cost to run one test task, US dollars at list prices.

size.height_basis: measured on the feasibility proof drawn to this spec (house faces, real logos, real rows); the final may differ by a little

exhibits.alt: Two charts of score against cost per task. Claude Opus 5.5 rises from 42.3 at Low ($0.55 a task) to 57.6 at Max ($5.98); Claude Opus 5, released two months earlier, runs from 39.4 to 50.8 and costs more at most levels. GPT-6 Sol rises from 28.5 with thinking off to 47.6 at Max; GPT-6.1 Sol, a week newer, runs from 42.1 at Low to 51.8 at Max and costs less at every level.
exhibits.after: The size of the gear change surprised me. Artificial Analysis, an independent group that tests these models, ran the same Claude Opus 5.5 through its long set of hard tests at different settings. Thinking as hard as it can, it scored more than a third higher than when thinking a little. The older Opus 5, at its hardest, beat the new one at its lowest. OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol, which OpenAI's help page says powers ChatGPT's thinking settings, scored about two thirds higher at its top developer setting than with thinking off, while the newer GPT-6.1 Sol at its top only edged past it. In both cases the gear moved the score more than the new badge did.

exhibits.source_line: Source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, read 17 Oct 2026. Cost per task in US dollars at list prices. Points and multiples: our arithmetic.

size.height_basis: measured on the feasibility proof drawn to this spec (house faces, real logos, real rows); the final may differ by a little

exhibits.alt: Six small line charts, one per model, of points added against cost as a multiple of the Low setting. Every line climbs steeply at first and flattens at each step. Claude Opus 5.5 adds 15.3 points for 10.9 times the cost; Claude Sonnet 5.5 adds 20.1 for 15.8 times; Claude Haiku 5.5 13.9 for 8.7 times; Claude Fable 5.1 6.6 for 3.2 times, its last step adding 0.2 points for 28% more; GPT-6.1 Sol 9.7 for 5.5 times; GPT-6 Sol 13.4 for 7.9 times.
exhibits.after: It isn't a straight line, though, and that matters for where this is heading. Each step up buys less than the one before. On Artificial Analysis's tests, moving Opus 5.5 from low to medium cost about two and a half times as much per task and brought the biggest jump in its score. Moving it from medium to max cost another four and a half times as much, for a smaller jump. Bottom to top, that's about 11 times the cost for a score just over a third higher. Every current model from Anthropic and OpenAI on those tests works the same way: the top setting costs several times more than the bottom one, and the score goes up by far less. The last step up is the worst deal of all. On Fable 5.1, it costs 28% more and barely moves the score. And the setting can beat the model. Claude Haiku 5.5, the cheapest of Anthropic's current models, on its highest setting edged past Opus 5.5 on its lowest, for less than half the cost per task. Sometimes the top gear even scores lower than the one below it. On Hex's data-analysis test, GPT-6 Sol scored 61.3% on its Xhigh (extra high) setting and 57% on Max, which costs more. Thinking can be pure waste, too: researchers asked reasoning models "what is the answer of 2 plus 3?" and found they "consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models to reach the same answer." (Tokens are the word pieces an AI reads and writes, and what developers pay for.) One wrote out 13 solutions. And sometimes the new name really is the bigger step. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 on its default setting "beats Opus 5 at max effort for about a fifth of the cost" on one test of computer tasks.

exhibits.question: Which buys more intelligence for the money: a new model version or a higher thinking level?
exhibits.heading: A new Claude Opus or GPT Sol adds fewer points than more thinking, but costs less
exhibits.standfirst: Points each change added on the Intelligence Index (0 to 100), and what it did to the cost per task.
exhibits.takeaway: On Artificial Analysis's 0 to 100 index, more thinking on the newest Claude Opus and GPT Sol added 9.7 to 15.3 points for 5.5 to 10.9 times the cost per task; the new version added 2.9 to 8.0 points at the same level and cost less at 9 of the 10 levels.

notes.text: GPT-6 Sol, from thinking off (Non-reasoning) to Max: +19.1 points for 3.1 times the cost. GPT-6.1 Sol has no thinking-off setting.
notes.placement: fine print under the OpenAI row

notes.text: Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol are now listed as deprecated; results as measured.

chart.type: a two by two grid of stat tiles (rows: Claude Opus, GPT Sol; columns: more thinking, new version), each with a big number, a bar on one shared points scale, and its cost
chart.why: The question is a straight comparison of two levers on two model lines, so a grid answers it at a glance: the left column's numbers and bars are longer, the right column's costs are lower. A bar chart with six labelled rows ran past 2,500 px at the phone floor.

encoding.grid: two columns of 600 px with a 32 px gutter; a two-line column head over each, 54 px ("More thinking" in mint over "same model"; "A new version" in cream over "same thinking level", second lines Archivo 500 at 70%); a row head with the company logo (56 px) and the model line (60 px Archivo 700) over each row
encoding.tile: #16221D fill, 12 px corners, 40 px padding; contents top to bottom: big number (Anton 104 px), what it is (54 px Archivo 500, up to 2 lines), bar, cost (54 px Archivo 700, up to 2 lines)
encoding.bar: one shared scale in every tile: 0 to 20 points over 520 px (26 px a point), 40 px tall, on a cream-at-14% track. More thinking: solid mint to the gain. New version: solid cream to the smallest gain across the five matched levels, then an unfilled 3 px cream outline to the largest, with a 12 px dot at each of the five gains (ink on the solid part, cream on the outline)
encoding.cost_colour: accent #FF6A4D where the change costs more, mint where it costs less

tiles.under: points, Opus 5.5 from Low to Max
points, Opus 5 to Opus 5.5 at each level
tiles.cost: 0.50 to 1.02 times the cost: cheaper at 4 of 5 levels

tiles.under: points, GPT-6.1 Sol from Low to Max
points, GPT-6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol at each level
tiles.cost: 0.69 to 0.98 times the cost: cheaper at every level

exhibits.source_line: Source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, read 17 Oct 2026. Cost per task in US dollars at list prices. Points and multiples: our arithmetic.

size.height_basis: measured on the feasibility proof drawn to this spec (house faces, real logos, real rows); the final may differ by a little

exhibits.alt: Four tiles. Claude Opus 5.5 from Low to Max adds 15.3 points for 10.9 times the cost; Opus 5 to Opus 5.5 at the same level adds 2.9 to 6.8 points at 0.50 to 1.02 times the cost. GPT-6.1 Sol from Low to Max adds 9.7 points for 5.5 times; GPT-6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol at the same level adds 4.2 to 8.0 points at 0.69 to 0.98 times the cost.
exhibits.after: That's also why a higher gear eats into your plan faster. Anthropic's help page for the Claude app says higher effort means responses "take longer and use more tokens, so you'll reach your usage limits faster." Changing model can do the same, but not always. Anthropic charges developers two and a half times as much for the same amount of writing from Fable 5.1, the model it points them to when Opus 5.5 falls short, as from Opus 5.5. A newer version often costs less, as the Opus 5.5 example above shows.

exhibits.question: If I need a given level of intelligence, which model and thinking level gets there cheapest, and where do the defaults land?
exhibits.heading: The cheapest route to each score mixes Claude and GPT models and thinking levels
exhibits.standfirst: For each score on the Intelligence Index (0 to 100), the current model and thinking level that reaches it at the lowest cost per task.
exhibits.takeaway: On Artificial Analysis's 0 to 100 index, scores up to 50 cost 12 to 32 cents a task at the cheapest; 55 takes Claude Opus 5.5 at Xhigh for $3.46, about 11 times as much, and Opus 5.5 on Anthropic's default (Medium) scores 51.2 for $1.34.

exhibits.alt: Price ladder. For a score of 40 or more the cheapest was Claude Haiku 5.5 at Xhigh (41.2, $0.12 a task) or GPT-6.1 Sol at Low (42.1, $0.13); 45 or more, GPT-6.1 Sol at Medium (47.8, $0.21); 50 or more, GPT-6.1 Sol at High (50.2, $0.32); 55 or more, Claude Opus 5.5 at Xhigh (56.0, $3.46); the top score, Claude Opus 5.5 at Max (57.6, $5.98). For comparison: Claude Opus 5.5 at its default, Medium, 51.2 for $1.34; Claude Haiku 5.5 at its default, Medium, 34.5 for $0.05; Gemini 4 Argon at High, 52.6 for $1.99.
exhibits.after: If you build products on AI, don't choose a model by its name or its launch chart. Run your own hard questions through each setting, check the answers, and watch how much thinking you pay for.

flags_for_krish.about: "Each step up buys less than the one before." (THE SWITCH THAT MATTERS)
flags_for_krish.finding: True on Artificial Analysis's data when "buys" means points per extra dollar: it holds at every step for all seven models listed at every setting, on both cost measures and on unrounded scores. In raw points it holds step by step for none of them: Claude Sonnet 5.5's Medium to High step (+6.0) added more than its Low to Medium step (+4.9), Fable 5.1's Medium to High (+2.3) more than Low to Medium (+2.1), Haiku 5.5's High to Xhigh (+3.4) more than Medium to High (+3.3), GPT-6 Sol's Xhigh to Max (+3.4) more than High to Xhigh (+1.8), and Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol each have two equal steps (+2.4 and +2.4; +0.8 and +0.8). What does hold in points: the top step adds less than the first for every one of them, and Opus 5.5's Low to Medium step is its biggest, as the article says. Exhibit 3 draws the per-dollar version and makes no step-by-step points claim, so it backs the sentence as written. No change to the article.

Every Artificial Analysis dollar figure and multiple in the article is cost per task ($5.98 v $0.55; "about two and a half times as much per task"; "another four and a half times"; "about 11 times"; "28% more"; "less than half the cost per task"), and Friday's video cards use cost per task too. An exhibit printed beside those sentences on the full-test-set cost would show 1.89, 5.35, 10.12, 1.45 and 0.38 times instead, so the reader would see two sets of numbers for one claim. data-final.json allows either, if the exhibit says which.

No source matches ChatGPT's app settings (Instant, Medium, High, Extra High) to Artificial Analysis's developer settings, and ChatGPT offers no Max, so no exhibit places ChatGPT's default. Exhibit 5 shows Anthropic's documented developer defaults only, and says why ChatGPT is not placed.
Artificial Analysis stars all five as understated; every exhibit showing a Haiku cost carries the line, and Exhibit 5 shows the 40 row as a near tie with GPT-6.1 Sol at Low.
